name: roman cheese pasta
instructions:
ROMAN CHEESE PASTA — cacio e pepe + alfredo merged 2026-11-13: the two roman cheese-emulsion pastas, one technique family (fine grate, starchy low-water boil, cheese in off the heat, loosen with pasta water). Variant A = CACIO E PEPE (pecorino + toasted pepper). Variant B = ALFREDO (butter + parmesan). The MUSHROOM ALFREDO idea is REMOVED — mushrooms are better in antipasti.

=== VARIANT A — CACIO E PEPE (PECORINO + PEPPER) ===

Cacio e pepe — the roman three-ingredient pasta: PECORINO ROMANO + BLACK PEPPER + PASTA WATER, emulsified into a sauce on the pasta. No butter, no oil, no cream in the classical build — the sauce is cheese + starch + water.

SERVES 2.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 8 oz (225g) spaghetti (or tonnarelli/bucatini)
- ~1 cup (100g) PECORINO ROMANO, finely grated (microplane or the smallest grater holes — fine matters for melting)
- 2 tsp whole black peppercorns, toasted and coarsely cracked (or ~1.5 tsp coarsely ground)
- salt (lightly — the pecorino is salty)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. TOAST THE PEPPER: crack the peppercorns and toast them in a dry skillet over medium heat until fragrant, ~1 min. Set the skillet aside (the pasta finishes in it).
2. COOK THE PASTA in LESS WATER THAN USUAL (just enough to cover — you want the water starchy) with a light hand on the salt. Pull it 1-2 minutes shy of al dente. RESERVE AT LEAST A CUP OF PASTA WATER before draining.
3. MAKE THE CHEESE PASTE: while the pasta cooks, mash the grated pecorino with a few tablespoons of the hot pasta water in a bowl to form a thick, smooth paste. This pre-emulsification step is the main insurance against clumping.
4. MARRY: add the pasta to the skillet with the toasted pepper and a splash of pasta water over LOW heat; toss ~1 min to finish cooking and coat with pepper.
5. OFF THE HEAT, add the cheese paste and toss/stir vigorously, loosening with more pasta water a splash at a time, until the sauce is glossy and clings. TOO-HIGH HEAT IS THE FAILURE MODE — pecorino seizes into clumps above ~150°F; the residual heat of the pasta is enough.
6. Serve immediately with more pecorino and cracked pepper on top. The sauce tightens as it sits — it does not hold or reheat.

=== VARIANT B — ALFREDO (BUTTER + PARMESAN) ===

The original roman dish (Alfredo di Lelio's fettuccine al burro): no cream, no garlic, no flour — the sauce is BUTTER + PARMESAN emulsified with starchy PASTA WATER on the noodles.

SERVES 2.

- 8 oz fettuccine
- 4 tbsp (57g) good butter, cubed
- ~1 cup (80-100g) PARMESAN, finely grated (microplane — fine grate melts evenly)
- salt (lightly — the parmesan is salty)

1. Cook the fettuccine in LESS WATER THAN USUAL (starchier water = better emulsion), lightly salted. Pull it just shy of al dente. RESERVE A CUP OF PASTA WATER.
2. In a warm (not hot) wide pan or bowl, toss the pasta with the butter and a splash of pasta water until the butter melts into a glossy coat.
3. OFF THE HEAT, add the parmesan in stages, tossing vigorously and loosening with pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce is creamy and clings. Same emulsion discipline as variant A (cacio e pepe) — too much direct heat and the cheese seizes.
4. Serve immediately — the sauce tightens as it sits and does not hold or reheat.
notes:
Both variants are PASSES (retagged 2026-11-13 after the first cooks; detailed findings not yet logged).

=== THE WHOLE FAMILY IS ONE EMULSION PROBLEM ===

Cacio e pepe is three ingredients and one technique problem: getting pecorino to emulsify with starchy water instead of seizing into chewing-gum clumps. The standard insurance, in order of importance:
1. CHEESE PASTE FIRST — mash the finely-grated pecorino with hot pasta water into a paste before it ever meets the pasta.
2. OFF-HEAT MARRIAGE — the cheese goes in off the flame; pecorino seizes when overheated.
3. STARCHY WATER — cook the pasta in less water than usual so the reserved water carries enough starch to stabilize the emulsion.
4. FINE GRATE — coarse shreds melt unevenly and clump before they disperse.

Parmesan is more forgiving than pecorino, which makes the alfredo variant the easier of the two to land.

=== THE CHEESE SPLIT — PECORINO IS A'S, PARMESAN IS B'S ===

Pecorino romano (sheep's milk, saltier, sharper) is the canonical cheese — it IS the 'cacio.' Parmesan melts more forgivingly and some recipes cut the pecorino with it as training wheels, but it reads sweeter/nuttier and the dish drifts away from its roman identity.

In the merged house: PECORINO ROMANO is variant A's cheese, PARMESAN is variant B's. Parmesan stays secondary for variant A only (the training-wheels cut).

=== PEPPER IS A CO-LEAD IN VARIANT A, NOT A SEASONING ===

The pepper is toasted and present in quantity — it's the second headliner, not a finishing grind. Toasting whole peppercorns and cracking them coarsely is the standard move for aroma plus bite.

=== VARIANT B IS THE REAL ALFREDO — NO CREAM ===

The italian original is a butter-and-parmesan emulsion on fresh fettuccine — the american cream-garlic-flour version is a different dish built on top of the name. This variant stays italian: butter + parmesan + pasta water, nothing else. (The americanized cream build now exists as its own recipe: [[american-chicken-alfredo]] — poached chicken, heavy cream, mozzarella, baked.)

=== THE MUSHROOM ALFREDO — REMOVED (2026-11-13) ===

The mushroom alfredo idea (shittake/chanterelle + garlic + thyme/oregano + lemon + crisped panko ON TOP of the finished emulsion, with the sogginess and flavor-leaking failure modes) is REMOVED: I think MUSHROOMS ARE BETTER IN ANTIPASTI ([[mushroom-antipasto]] is the antipasti mushroom home). This also walks back the earlier 'shittakes work well in a standard alfredo' idea — untested, now withdrawn. The standing stance is unchanged: I tend to DISLIKE PURE CREAM + MUSHROOM sauces, indian, italian, or otherwise (the tomato-might-help question retired with boscaiola). Full mushroom-build text survives in git history.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[sardine-parsley-antipasti]]: the other lean, few-ingredient build — same genre of pasta-water-emulsion technique doing the heavy lifting.
- [[mushroom-antipasto]]: where the mushroom urge goes now (antipasti, not pasta).
